newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bankgesellschaft up on risk disclosure.
newsitem.headline: Bankgesellschaft up on risk disclosure.

text.p: Shares in Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG surged more than eight percent on Monday as analysts welcomed the bank's prompt move to set aside 2.2 billion marks ($1.4 billion) this year to cover problem loans.

The shares closed up 2.05 marks or 8.1 percent at 27.30 marks on the Frankfurt stock exchange as several analysts upgraded their stock recommendations in reaction to its surprise announcement on Friday.
The shares have slumped more than 30 percent from a March peak of 39.85 marks on worries about the bank's earnings.
"People are saying the worst may be over now," said Nathalie Grasegger, banking analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank.

Bankgesellschaft's move to cover the loans, which were caused by a slump in its core region of Berlin and east Germany, followed a decision by Union Bank of Switzerland last week to set aside 4.4 billion francs ($3.4 billion) for its risk loans.

But analysts warned it remained unclear whether Bankgesellschaft had covered all risks and questioned how it would be able to meet a pledge to pay an unchanged dividend as well as post a break-even result for 1996 despite the provision.
With insolvencies in east Germany unlikely to ebb next year, Bankgesellschaft will have to maintain high provisions, the analysts said.
They added the bank would probably see its interest income squeezed next year by increased caution in extending new loans.

The Berlin bank, which is considering a merger or tie-up in some form with Norddeutsche Landesbank, also said its two chief executives, Wolfgang Steinriede and Hubertus Moser, would quit the board at the end of the year.
They will be replaced by management board member Wolfgang Rupf on January 1 next year, who had originally been scheduled to take the post later in the year.

"Bankgesellschaft has probably done all it could to enable Rupf to start out with clean accounts," said Christine Winkler, an analyst at Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank, who has upgraded her recommendation to hold from sell.
But she added: "It is unclear if they have covered all risks and how risk provisions will develop in the coming years. We need more details."
Dieter Hein, banking analyst at BHF Bank in Frankfurt, raised his Bankgesellschaft recommendation to buy from hold, saying its shares were undervalued based on projections for its 1998 earnings.
He revised his 1996 forecast to a loss of two marks per share from an earlier prediction of a 1.60 mark profit, but raised his 1997 profit forecast to 3.20 marks from 2.30.

The bank, 56.8 percent-owned by the state of Berlin, last month reported a 32.4 percent slide in operating earnings in the first nine months caused by galloping costs, high risk provisions and a 56 million-mark loss from own-account trading.
It set aside 819 million marks in gross risk provisions for the first nine months and warned last month that the slump in its home region was showing no signs of abating.
Hit by a downturn in the real estate market, Berlin's economy has fared worse than all other German regions this year with firms collapsing at a rate far above the national average.
Spiegel magazine reported in Monday's edition that the credit risks at Bankgesellschaft came to light during merger negotiations with Norddeutsche Landesbank.
Both banks had agreed to disclose all their risks as a basis for valuing the banks, the report said.
A Bankgesellschaft spokeswoman denied the report, saying no auditors had been commissioned yet to value the banks.

In a move which fuelled speculation about mergers in Germany's overcrowded banking sector, the two banks in October got the go-ahead from their state owners to intensify talks about increasing cooperation. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($1=1.5414 Mark) ($1=1.3108 Swiss Franc)
